fields.meta_description: Build a health screening form that alerts a named person on every yes, with each answer saved to a database you own. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Health Screening Form That Flags Who Needs Follow-Up
fields.hero_description: Say who answers and who follows up on a yes. Emergent builds the health screening form and the records each answer lands in.
fields.features_heading: What Screening Forms Need Past the Questions
fields.features_subheading: Printed versions stop at the questions. These are the parts that act on the answers.
fields.feature_1:
A yes goes to one named person

Each yes triggers an email or Slack alert to the person who handles it. A reported symptom reaches the nurse on shift, and the person who answered sees the next step on screen.
fields.feature_2:
Staff fields for the readings

Add fields a nurse or volunteer fills in after the questions, such as a blood pressure reading or a vision result. Each one saves to the record that holds the earlier answers.
fields.feature_3:
Counts for managers, answers for nurses

Choose who reads individual answers and who gets a total instead. A program manager can see that 212 people took part that day without opening a single reading or questionnaire.
fields.feature_4:
Short screens for a phone

Show one or two questions per screen. A parent in the pickup line or a visitor at a door can finish on a phone, and a yes opens its follow-up question on the next screen.
fields.feature_5:
Each screening kept as a dated row

Store every screening as a dated row that holds the answers and the outcome. Pull every visitor screened last Tuesday, or every student due for a recheck, with one filter.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can take with you

Export the full code for the form and its database to your GitHub repository. A developer can host it on your own servers or connect it to any clinic or HR system with an API.

fields.tab_content_1:
Readings go to each employee and a headcount to HR

Northwind Logistics holds a screening day each spring at its Reno warehouse. Employees fill in the questionnaire before their slot, and a vendor nurse enters blood pressure, glucose and cholesterol on site. Results go to each employee by email. HR sees 212 of 340 employees screened, with no individual readings.
fields.tab_content_2:
Vision results that reach parents by the final bell

Maple Grove Elementary screens vision and hearing for every Grade 2 class in a single morning. Nurse Carla Diaz marks each student Pass or Refer as the line moves. A Refer emails the parent before dismissal with the matching referral form attached, and the student's row records that the notice went out.
fields.tab_content_3:
Blood pressure taken in line, referral in hand

The Riverside County Fair health booth posts a QR code at the back of the line. Visitors answer the questions on their phone while they wait. The volunteer nurse only takes a blood pressure reading. When the nurse marks a reading for follow-up, the phone shows a referral sheet for the nearest community clinic.
fields.tab_content_4:
With one yes at the door, the visit waits

Visitors at Cedar Hill Care Home scan a code at the front door and answer three questions about symptoms in the past two days. Three no answers put a green pass on the front desk screen. Any yes holds the visit and sends an in-app alert to Grace Owens, the charge nurse on duty.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Health Screening Form
fields.howto_description: Building it takes one prompt. Most of the thinking goes into what the form decides and who hears about a yes.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Name the decision the form makes
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Add the fields staff fill in
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Route each yes to a person
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down what the screening decides: go ahead, wait or refer. A care home deciding on a visit needs a handful of questions. A wellness day that hands out results needs a questionnaire plus measurement fields. Anything that does not feed the decision is optional.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Drop every question whose answer would not change the outcome. For current employees, EEOC guidance sets a narrow test for medical questions. Have whoever handles HR or legal check the list against that test before the form goes out.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Some answers come from staff, not the form. Give nurses and volunteers their own fields for readings like blood pressure or a vision result, saved to the same record. Mark which fields the person screened can see and which stay with staff.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Pick who acts on each answer that needs follow-up, and whether the alert arrives by email or in Slack. Name a person, not a shared inbox. Show the person screened a plain next step on screen while that alert goes out.
fields.howto_step_5_des: List the people who need individual answers and those who need only a count. The EEOC expects employee medical information to sit in separate, confidential files, apart from personnel records. A program manager usually needs participation numbers, not anyone's readings.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Paste the questions and the alert rules into the prompt. Emergent builds the form and the database table behind it. When a question changes next season, edit it with another prompt instead of reprinting a stack of copies.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Fill it in on a phone as someone with no symptoms and again as someone who answers yes. Then enter a reading as staff. Check that each alert reaches the named person and that a count-only viewer sees no individual answers.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is printable paper: a Carepatron test PDF, a school district's screening notice, a class sign-up sheet that says hand it to your instructor, a county coverage form and two physician forms for wellness programs. Each one asks the questions and stops there. A screening form exists to reach a decision, go ahead or follow up, and to send that decision to one person while the answers stay with whoever is allowed to hold them. This page shows what to ask, where the decision sits and who sees what, in four settings the SERP points at: an employer screening day, school vision and hearing checks, a health fair booth and a care home's visitor door check.
tab_stories: At a company wellness screening day, employees answer the questionnaire before their slot, a nurse enters the measurements, each employee receives their own results and HR only sees how many people took part.
A school nurse records vision and hearing results for a whole grade, and every student who does not pass gets a notice sent to a parent with a referral form attached.

Visitors at a county fair health booth answer the questions on their phone while they wait, a volunteer nurse adds the blood pressure reading, and anyone the nurse marks for follow-up leaves with a referral sheet for the nearest clinic.
A care home asks every visitor three symptom questions at the door, and any yes holds the visit and messages the charge nurse on duty before the visitor walks in.

claims_to_source: Health screenings look for diseases before symptoms appear; blood pressure checks and cholesterol tests are common examples
A workplace health screening usually pairs a health risk questionnaire with biometric measurements such as height, weight, blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose
Under the ADA, once someone is employed, an employer may ask disability-related questions or require medical exams only when they are job-related and consistent with business necessity
Medical information about employees must be kept on separate forms, in separate medical files, and treated as confidential
Nursing texts describe four types of health assessment: initial, focused, emergency and time-lapsed
